analysis.one_liner: Bans the IRS's free Direct File tax return filing program.
analysis.headline: The bill shutting down the IRS's free Direct File program has had no action since being referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the tax code to prohibit the Treasury Secretary from preparing or filing federal tax returns, written specifically to shut down the IRS Direct File program, which lets taxpayers in 25 states file their federal returns free through the IRS website [S2]. Taxpayers could still use the IRS Free File program, which routes people to third-party tax software companies, or the Volunteer Income Tax Assistance program run with local community groups [S2]. The bill also bars Treasury from awarding grants or contracts to build or run any government electronic tax preparation service [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Senator Blackburn with 10 Republican cosponsors and has sat in the Finance Committee since January 2025 [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial tax preparation software companies gain the most: the bill removes Direct File, the free government-run competitor, and steers filers toward the Free File program that runs through their own products [S2]. Taxpayers who prefer to file without the IRS involved would also get what they want, but the bill does not create any new option for them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes the Direct File program out of law by prohibiting the Secretary of the Treasury from preparing tax returns and defining any IRS-run electronic tax preparation service as prohibited preparation [S3].

It leaves two existing free channels intact: the IRS Free File program, which uses third-party tax software, and the Volunteer Income Tax Assistance grant program for low-income, disabled, and limited-English taxpayers [S2].

It also blocks Treasury from spending money on grants, contracts, or agreements to develop or operate a government electronic tax preparation service, preventing the program from being rebuilt under another name [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers who use Direct File in the 25 participating states would lose the free, direct way to file with the IRS and would have to switch to third-party software, which may cost money or involve upselling [S2]. All taxpayers keep funding the IRS while the agency is barred from offering the service it built.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers using Direct File in 25 states

drawbacks.text: Direct File is free to use; ending it takes away a no-cost filing option and can push filers toward paid software or upsold 'free' services, a real cost for working households each tax season [S2].

The bill defines preparation so broadly that the IRS could not complete even part of a return for a taxpayer, limiting help the agency could offer beyond the specific carve-outs for Free File and VITA [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection in favor is that a government agency both writing the tax rules and preparing the returns creates a conflict of interest and duplicates what private software already does for free through Free File; supporters would also note the bill preserves VITA for people who genuinely need hands-on help [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall directly on ordinary filers, who would lose the one truly free, direct filing channel and likely end up paying commercial software companies or navigating upsells instead. The benefits go almost entirely to the tax preparation industry, whose market Direct File competes with. The bill does preserve VITA and Free File, but Free File itself runs through the same companies that benefit from Direct File's elimination, so the net effect is a transfer from taxpayers to that industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2025 and has seen no further action since, so it has not been voted on and Direct File still operates.

narrative.text: Senator Blackburn introduced the FAIR PREP Act on January 15, 2025, joined by 10 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and the action history shows no hearings, markup, or floor action since [S5].
Because no amendment has been enacted, the IRS Direct File program continues to operate for qualified taxpayers in 25 participating states [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, nobody has changed position: Direct File is still running, and the tax prep industry's market remains intact but unsecured until a law says so. If the bill ever advances, the software companies gain a permanent, legal shield against their free public competitor.

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit IRS return preparation and end Direct File.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrat has signed on, and the bill has not reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record to measure the split.

industries.industry: Tax preparation software companies (Intuit, H&R Block and peers)
industries.note: The bill bans Direct File, the free government-run filing option that competes directly with these companies' products, and steers filers to Free File, which routes taxpayers through their own software. Their gain comes at the expense of filers who would otherwise file free with the IRS.
The bill explicitly preserves the VITA grant program, so community organizations that provide free tax help keep their funding and role; they neither gain nor lose materially.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a small all-Republican cosponsor bloc and has not moved since its January 2025 referral to Finance, with no hearing or markup scheduled. Bills at this stage with no committee activity rarely reach the floor on their own; the realistic path to enactment would be attachment to a larger tax package, and in the meantime Direct File continues operating.
